LICENSING MEETING.
A special licensing meeting for the purpose of
dealing with the application for renewals of publicans'
licenses in the metropolitan district, was held at the
Water Police Court yesterday, when Mr. A. M. Fisher
and Mr. John Macintosh, L.M.'s., were present.
There are in all 858 public houses in the metropolitan district, and there were over 300 applications for renewals of publicans' licenses.
Eight of the applications were objected to ;
the remainder were granted. Transfers of publicans' licenses were granted as follows:- From
Sebastian Hodge (deceased) to Emily H. Hodge
(widow), for the Commercial Hotel, King and
Castlereagh streets; Elizabeth Haddon to E. J.
Hughes, Glen Hotel, Liverpool - street ; John
Monat to Michael Bourke, Empire Hotel,
Sussex-Street ; Thomas Foster Knox (trading as
Dalgety and Co., Limited) was granted a spirit merchant's license. A packet license was issued to H.
Bennison. The spirit merchant's license of Robert
Cunynghame (trading as Cunynghame and Co.,
Limited, Bond-street) was transferred to Vaughan,
Rogers, and Co. A number of music permits, booth,
hawkers', and pawnbrokers' licenses were also issued.
The application of Charles H. E. Lindeman for a
renewal of publican's license for the Ropemaker's
Arms, George-street North, was opposed by Sub-Inspector
Atwill on the ground that certain alterations
had been effected in the property for which the license
was originally granted which tended to render the
place unfit for an hotel. Mr. Slattery, for the applicant, contended that Lindeman's house possessed all the
accommodation required by the Act. The Bench expressed a desire to visit the premises in question, and
the further hearing of the matter was postponed for a
week. John Cooper, licensee of the Metropolitan Hotel,
George-street, applied for a renewal of his license. The
application was opposed by Sub-Inspector Atwill on
the ground that the applicant was a man of intemperate
habits. After hearing evidence, the Bench said they
had no desire to take Cooper's license from him, but
hoped this would be a warning to him in future. The
application was granted. The other applications for
renewals which have been objected to by the police will
he heard at future sittings of the Licensing Court.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.13710000:
COUNTRY NEWS.
-
[BY TELEGRAPH.
FROM OUR CORRESPONDENTS.)
BRAIDWOOD, FRIDAY.
A complimentary banquet was given last night to
Mr. J. T. Murphy, previous to his leaving the district.
About 40 leading citizens were present. Mr. R.
Hassall being in the chair. The health of the guest
was drunk with much enthusiasm.
BYROCK, FRIDAY.
The Rev. J. B. Gribble, who has travelled across the
country from the Barwon mission station, arrived here
last night with a party of blacks; he goes on to Dubbo
to-day to gather up the natives in that district. There
are 85 aborigines settled at the mission.
COBAR, FRIDAY.
Business at the local Government office for the past
year shows a marked increase over that of the preceding year. At the local police court 491 cases were
dealt with. The revenue received, exclusive of lands,
was £6494 12s. 7d., being an increase over the preceding year of £3504 9s. 5d. At the warden's office
(mining), 42 gold applications, embracing 391 acres,
and 195 mineral applications, covering 1726 acres, were
received, the revenue received being £3334 2s. In
every department the increase has been most pronounced.
FORBES, FRIDAY. .
The revenue of Forbes Land Office for the year 1888
was nearly £20,000.
GUNDAGAI, FRIDAY.
The receipts at the Crown Lands Office, Gundagai,
for the quarter ending December were £1989 1s. 8d.
INVERELL, FRIDAY.
The revenue for the year at the Lands Office was
£16,364 13s. 2d.
Mr. J. H. Michell, hotelkeeper, and a very old resident of Tingha, died to-day.
NARRANDERA, FRIDAY.
In response to a large requisition, the Mayor has
convened a public meeting for this evening to consider
what steps shall be taken to procure the railway extension to the Lachlan. The proposed line would open up
a large area of agricultural land, that would be readily
selected once it was made accessible.
NEWCASTLE, FRIDAY.
This morning Constable Anderson, of Adamstown,
apprehended a man named Thos. Robertson on a charge
of forgery at Armidale. He was brought up at the local
police court to-day and remanded to Armidale.
WELLINGTON, FRIDAY.
At yesterday's annual meeting for the election of a
hospital committee, medical officer, &c., only the secretary put in an appearance, and he, after waiting
an hour, adjourned the meeting until next
week. It is rumoured that Dr. Rygate does
not intend to renew his connection with the hospital, which has existed for upwards of 20 years. The
treasurer has resigned, and it is thought that the institution will have to be closed. Interest in all public
matters is at a very low ebb here.
WINDSOR, FRIDAY.
A very old resident of Windsor, Mrs. Ann Collins,
96 years of age, was found dead in bed yesterday. An
inquest was held to-day, and a verdict of death from
natural causes was returned.
At Pitt Town, Mr. S. Cox has struck water at a
depth of 24 feet on his farm. It is believed that all
the farmers in the vicinity could be similarly successful.
Little surprise is expressed here at the resignation of
the Government. Mr. Bowman's friends are expecting
him to visit the electorate shortly.
WARDELL, FRIDAY.
John M'Lean and his old trainer, Charles Tyler,
arrived here yesterday, and were met on the wharf by a
number of friends. In the evening they were banqueted at the Star Hotel. The town was decorated
with bunting, red, white, and blue predominating.
The Wardell brass band played through the town until
a late hour.
A young girl named Annie Palmer met with a serious
accident to-day. While taking a pot off the fire her
clothes ignited. Her hands and body were severely
burned. She is under the care of Dr. Tomlins, and
now lies in a critical condition.

The Caledonians journeyed down to Helensburgh on
Saturday last to encounter the Helensburgh Rovers,
and a one-sided game resulted in a win for the
Caledonians by 7 goals to nil. The visitors were afterwards entertained to supper, and spent a very enjoyable
evening. The Caledonians, under skipper Gleghorn,
comprised Logan, Aiken, Ferguson, Todd, Greig,
Mathieson, Philips, Irvine, and Murray, and they were
accompanied by a number of friends.
The Parkgrove Club (playing under Southern British
Association rules) journeyed to Balgownie, near Wollongong, on Queen's Birthday, to try conclusions with
the local club. The visitors were met at
the station by several members of the club.
The match formed part of a programme
of sports which were well patronised. The Parkgrove
captain having won the toss, decided to play for the
first half with wind and sun in his favour. The ball
having been set in motion, was carried down to the
locals' goal, but was well returned, and some nice play
in mid-field resulted. Several times the visitors had
excellent chances of scoring, but owing to their bad
shooting and the splendid play of the Balgownie backs,
their efforts were in vain.' The game throughout the
first half was of a very even nature, and the teams
were well matched. Half-time was called without
either side having scored, although strenuous efforts
were made on the part of both teams. For some time
after the ball was sent rolling again the play was very
equal, but the ball having been run down the field by
Connors and Thompson, the Parkgrove had the luck to
score out of a scrimmage in front of the Balgownie
goal. This put the local team on its mettle, and for
some time the visitors' citadel was in great danger,
being only saved by the splendid play of the goalkeeper, Dunstan. From this till the call of time the
game waxed fast and furious, and the local players
were having the better of it when the whistle sounded
for cessation of hostilities, the scores being-Parkgrove, 1 goal: Balgownie, nil. The visitors were
royally entertained after the match, everything possible
being done for their comfort and enjoyment. The remainder of the stay was occupied by a visit to the
famed Bulli Pass and excursions round the neighbourhood, which were thoroughly enjoyed.

NORTH SYDNEY RAILWAY.
PUBLIC MEETING AT ST. LEONARDS.
A public meeting of the residents and ratepayers of
North Shore was held last evening at the Masonic
Hall, St. Leonards, to discuss and consider the advisableness of assisting and co-operating with the
North Sydney, Manly, and Pittwater Railway Extension League. The attendance, which numbered about
80, was presided over by the Mayor of St. Leonards,
Mr. F. Punch. Two of the members for the district,
Messrs. Burns and Cullen, were present.
The Chairman explained that the railway to be
considered was one which would run over the populous
district of North Shore. He thought that if the North
Shore people showed the Government by fair and
reasonable arguments that the railway would be a good
and paying one, it would cause the project
to be put before the Public Works Committee.
Again, if the line were constructed, it would not
only be a paying concern, but would increase the value
of thousands of acres land owned by the Government to
an enormous extent. He regretted that the evening
was a wet one. Had it been fine many more would
have been present ; still, he knew that those who were
away would enter heart and soul into the movement.
Among the apologies which he had received
was one from the Hon. E. Barton, M.L.C.
Mr. F. A. A. Wilson moved,—"That this meeting
approves of the action of the North Sydney, Manly,
and Pittwater Railway Extension League in endeavouring to secure the establishment of railway communication between North Sydney, Manly, and Pittwater."
He contended that there was a necessity for the railway, and that the line would open up a vast amount of
good country.
Mr. D. Thomson seconded the resolution, and said
it had his heartiest sympathy. In spite of the difficulties of access the district of the Hawkesbury was even
now going ahead, and only required proper communication to make it a residential centre. If the Govern-
ment would take steps to secure now the ground which
would be required for the railway, it would save
the country a great deal of money. The Government
would, proportionately, get the railway for nothing
if it made the line now instead of waiting for years
until the route to be taken should be settled upon by a
number of residents. It did not need any foresight to
see that the district must go ahead, and that there
would in time be as large a city on this side of the
harbour as there was now on the other.
Mr. Burns, who supported the resolution, said that
he desired to manifest by his presence, rather than by
making a speech his sympathy with the cause. The
policy of the residents was to gather information and
get the Government to ask Parliament to send the proposal on to the Public Works Committee. He also
briefly commended the project in similar terms to those
in which he recently advocated it at Manly, and added
that he had ascertained that the population of the three
principal boroughs on the North Shore had increased
129 per cent. in the last eight years.
Mr. Cullen said he considered that the people of
Manly and Pittwater were entitled to the railway
on the ground of the present importance of
those places. He would give some figures to
show why the railway should be constructed.
He found that the population of North Shore and
Manly was 22,500. The steamer passenger traffic
between Sydney and Manly amounted to about 350,000
or 400,000 passengers per annum. Between Manly and
Newport during the summer months of the year, the
number of passengers was about 6000, while the number
of coach journeys for the same period was about 4000.
Between Manly and North Shore, although up to a
few months ago the communication was of a most
forbidding character, there were 5800 passengers in six months. For the six months
after the new punt was put on the passengers
numbered 9300. These were significant facts.
The unalienated acreage of Government Crown lands
at Manly Cove, Narrabeen, and Broken Bay was about
36,500 acres, and at least half of this would be
materially increased in value the moment the line was
made. In conclusion, he pointed to the rapidly
increased settlement in the localities served by the
suburban portion of the Illawarra line immediately
that line was constructed.
The resolution, on being put, was carried unanimously.
Mr. W. T. Muston moved,—"That the following
gentlemen be appointed to represent this district at the
meetings of the league :—Mr. F. Punch, Mayor of St.
Leonards; Mr. J. Mountford, Mayor of East St.
Leonards; Mr. M. McMahon, Mayor of Victoria; Mr.
W. T. Muston, Mayor of Willoughby; Messrs.
Joseph Waterhouse, G. T. Clarke, J. R. Carey, A.
Muston, F. A. A. Wilson, J. Monday, and W. C.
Woolcott."
Mr. M. McMahon, in seconding the resolution, urged
that the Government should construct the line on
sanitary grounds, the country which would be opened
up would yield healthy homes for the population. Some
of the most lovely country in the world was to be found
at Pittwater. No other such country near Sydney
could be opened to the public. The proposed railway
should not cost more than £10,000 per mile, and there
would be about 20 miles of it.
The resolution was unanimously carried.
On the motion of Mr. T. S. M'Cormick, a subscription
list to provide the sinews of war was opened, and, at
the request of the Mayor of Manly, the chairman was
accorded a vote of thanks.

THE GOLD DEPOSITS OF PERU.
Sir Charles Mansfield, the British Minister at Lima,
has recently sent to the Foreign Office an elaborate report on the auriferous deposits of Peru, drawn from the
report of the Lima School of Mining. In the mountain ranges of Peru, in the vicinity of the seaboard, whenever the rocks are of a crystalline character, gold is found in veins of
quartz which have been intruded into the
granite and syenite. In this belt almost all the spurs
of the Andes are of those formations, and the auriferous
quartz is almost invariably accompanied by oxide of
iron and mica. The proportion of oxide of iron varies
considerably. Every possible form is met with, from
white quartz permeated with small ferruginous spots to
a reddish rock so charged with oxide of iron that
it forms almost the whole of the auriferous mineral,
the quartz appearing, as it were, in an accidental
manner. The quartz in the auriferous minerals of the
coast varies considerably in appearance, being found
crystallised in prisms, in semi-crystallised grains,
agglomerated with and united by oxide of iron, or in
amorphous masses more or less compact, or friable,
with the appearance of scoria. In this district the
auriferous quartz is often associated with other
minerals, such as a white talcose substance, smooth to
the touch, with a silky, almost silvery polish, with
flakes of carbonate of lime of a laminar structure, and
limonite of a resinous appearance. Lastly, on the coast
of Peru gold may sometimes be discerned in copper
minerals, as well as in those mixed with chalk, copper
pyrites, malachite, alacamite, and silicate of copper, in
the upland districts, where the formations exhibit the
character of aqueous deposits, veins of gold
are not only found in crystalline earths, but
also in metamorphic rocks, such as quartzites and slaty
schist, intruding themselves into the sedimentary and
eruptive formations. In these veins the gold is sometimes in a pure state, as well as in pyrites, sulphuret
of iron, or accompanied by other metallic sulphurets
more or less auriferous, copper pyrites, panabasa,
bournonite, galena, jamesonite, &c. Gold in the
mountain range is found in veins and threads, and in
the alluvial districts of the same in flakes and grains.
In the Cordillera Oriental, in the district called the
Montana, gold is usually found in quartz veins injected into talc and clay slate by upheaval of crystalline rocks. The quartz which accompanies the gold
in this district is white, and occasionally exhibits
marks of oxide of iron, but the latter is never found
in the same abundance as in the auriferous minerals
of the seaboard. In this part of Peru there are important beds of auriferous soil, and it is from here
that the greater number of nuggets have been extracted. The report then passes in review all the districts of the country where, as far as is known at
present, the existence of gold has been authenticated
following the departments in geographical succession
from north to south. The information is given in
great detail, and refers to all the mines, worked and
worked, and gold deposits known to exist in Peru,
with details respecting the quantity of the metal
obtainable. This portion of the report occupies 26 pages.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.13852000:
THE CONCILIATION AND ARBITRATION ACT.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD
Sir, - The weakness of the Trade Disputes Conciliation and Arbitration Act, at the very point
where it should be strong, is demonstrated to us, and
clearly so, by the present strike at Broken Hill, for
were the Act in operation at the present moment it
could not be made use of, as one side to the dispute
refuses to submit to arbitration. The same thing
will happen, it appears to me, in all trade disputes of
any magnitude. Then the question arises whether
as we have admitted the principle of legislative interference in trade disputes, we should compel one
side to a dispute to submit to a desire expressed by
the other side for arbitration, as could be done by
admitting into the above Act the principle of compulsion. In passing this Act the Legislature of the
colony have given their sanction to the principle of
Parliamentary interference in trade disputes, and
may it not be as well to entrench that principle in its
strongest position by making the Act compulsory?
There can be little doubt but what the Act will be
taken advantage of only when there is little to be
lost or gained by either side to a dispute, but when
it would be of the greatest use to the whole community it will probably be ignored. Thus we have
our Statute Book loaded with another Act weak in
its operation, and can we not with justice trace the
cause of this to too great a desire for new laws,
regardless of their effectiveness? It is as if we
were to say let us have new legislation, in fact
any legislative measures so long as they are new.
The usefulness - or, rather, the ineffectiveness - of
this Act gives us the impression that legislative
measures are being placed on the Statute Book before
the people have had time to maturely consider the
principles embodied in them, and it is question
whether we should not protest against the colony
being put to the expense of passing laws which we
found inoperative, where they are mostly desired to
be of use. I am &c.,
July 7. SAMUEL BROOKS.

owner of the Strawberry Hills 'buses stating that

Supreme Court.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.13991000:
THE CASE OF JOHN COPP.
ATTEMPTS TO SOLVE THE MYSTERY.
THE BODY TO BE EXHUMED.
Yesterday morning the Minister for Justice (Mr.
A. J. Gould) received his final report in regard to
the case of John Copp, including one from the Chief
Medical Adviser to the Government After having
read the reports, Mr Gould decided to issue orders
for the exhumation of Copp's body, and for the
holding of a post-mortem examination of it. In-
structions were accordingly sent to the City Coroner,
and arrangements were made-for the body
to be exhumed at an early hour this morning,
in the presence of Dr Rennie (Government
Pathologist), Dr. Goode, and Mr Hamlet
(Government Analyst). The Inspector-General of
Police has also been communicated with to secure the
co-operation of the police in regard to the exhuma-
tion of the body, and also in regard to making any
further inquiries that may tend to throw light on the
circumstances connected with Copp's death.
The body was buried in the Church of England
portion of the Rookwood Cemetery on the 3rd
December, 1891. The number of the grave is 920,
section CC. For some time the police have been in-
vestigating the matter, and Detective Hinds has been
instructed to supervise the work of exhumation. When
the work has been completed, the body will be
brought to the South Sydney Morgue, where Drs.
Rennie and Goode will perform an autopsy. Por-
tions of the body are then to be submitted to the
Government Analyst (Mr Hamlet). The exhumation
is to be begun, as stated, at an early hour this morn-
ing, and it is anticipated that the arrangements will
be speedily carried out. Upon the result of the
autopsy and of the analysis any future action by the
police in the matter will largely depend.
Copp, it will be remembered, was in Thornton's
Half-way House, Botany on the night previous to
his death. The following morning he was found in
an unconscious state by two boys on a piece of land
now included in Rosebery Park. The boys directed
the attention of a constable named Manuell to Copp,
and the constable conveyed him to Prince Alfred
Hospital at 6. 30 a.m. He died in the hospital two
hours after admission. The entry-book at the in-
stitution describes the deceased as having been in a
state of coma when admitted but it does
not give any further particulars. There
were no marks of violence on Copp's body,
but Dr Purser, of the institution, declined to give
a certificate that death had resulted from natural
canses unless a post-mortem examination were
made. Drs Hunter and Munro, however, gave a
certificate but it had been represented to the
doctors that an autopsy would be distasteful to
members of Copp's family. It was also known that
Copp suffered from epileptic fits - a fact which
strengthened the impression of his death from
natural causes. He is spoken of as being a man of
sober habits and good behaviour.
It is impossible to say what proceedings will be the
result of the action of the authorities in issuing the
order for exhumation. It is certain that there are
circumstances connected with the matter that call
for investigation and those who are entrusted with
the case are fully seized of this but the great diffi-
culty in the matter is, even if it be ascertained that
Copp did not meet his death by natural causes or by
accident, to connect anyone with the affair. If the
result of the analysis of the body prove that Copp
met his death by being poisoned, then the detectives
will continue their investigations.

SALVATION ARMY.
A united officers and soldiers' meeting will be
held in the Salvation Army Temple, Goulburn-street,
next week, at which the question of General Booth's
visit to the colony will be considered. Lieutenant
Colonel Hoskin will preside, assisted by Major Taylor
(the colony secretary), and Majors Graham and
Wossberg (Sydney divisional officers).
General Booth has been compelled to postpone his
visit to Tasmania and New Zealand on account of
serious indisposition, His medical advisers insist on
this course being taken. It is hoped he will be
sufficiently recovered to undertake his New South
Wales campaign, which he purposes commencing
early in April
In connection with General Booth's projected visit
to Sydney the Railway Commissioners have granted
return tickets at single fares from all stations on
production of a Salvation Army certificate duly
signed. A similar concession has been made by the
North Coast S N Company to those travelling
saloon to the general's meetings.
To celebrate General Booth's seventieth birthday
it has been decided by the Salvation Army to endeavour to gain some 7000 new soldiers besides other
important work undertaken on the plan of advance,
to be consummated by the end of the century.
Ensign Minnie Rowell, editress of the " Young
Soldier," the Salvation Army junior soldiers' paper,
who has been recently indisposed, is on furlough in
New South Wales. She is progressing favourably,
although it is considered it will be some time ere she
is fit for work again.

STATEMENT BY MR. CATER.
Mr. Cater, of the Bellambi Colliery, returned to
Sydney yesterday morning, and gave the particulars
to a " Herald " representative. He said : " When
the vessel struck there were about 100 people on the
beach ; but no attempt was made to save life as
there was no apparatus available, and boats could
not live in the heavy sea. None of the crew were
successful in reaching the shore, but one man,
hanging on a plank, drifted within a few yards of
the shore, when he was immediately washed out to
sea again." About 18 months ago the Amy was
driven ashore near Cronulla Beach.
The Amy was owned by Messrs. Warburton and
Sons, Sydney. The first person to observe the vessel
appears to have been Mr. M'Cauley, a son of a
farmer, after whom the beach was named. He was
engaged in rounding up some cows, when he was
amazed to see the Amy's masts looming up but a
short distance away. The wind was blowing a gale
from the E.S.E., with thick rain, and as the ill-
fated vessel canted over in the surf the waves swept
her fore and aft. No help could possibly have been
rendered from the shore, so tempestuous was the
weather and sea, as there were no means
of communicating with the crew. The brig
had her main and fore lower topsails set.
Very little was seen of the eight persons on board.
Captain M'Gee, the master, was noticed by an
onlooker in the rigging. Of the two boats on the
brig one was launched, but no sooner was she
lowered than she was swamped, and the sole
occupant of the boat, who, it is surmised, was the
winchman, was swept away. The man secured a
plank, and after being tossed about in the very heavy
sea disappeared. Some of the others were discerned in the rigging and on the bowsprit. Had a
life-saving apparatus or lines been available it is
considered that some lives would have been saved.
The master was well known here, and was about
55 years of age and a very careful and experienced
mariner. The others lost were a mate, cook, winchman, and four sailors.

ANTARCTIC EXPLORATION.
THE BRITISH EXPEDITION.
LONDON, May 18.
" Nature," in commenting upon the
differences that arose in regard to the command of the projected expedition to the Antarctic regions, blames the council of the
Royal Geographical Society for refusing to
endorse the compromise which Mr. R. A.
Gregory had accepted.
Professor E. B. Poulton accuses some of
the committee-men of the Royal Society of
having sacrificed an exceptionally competent
Antarctic scientific leader for the sake of
peace.
In February last a discussion arose between the
Royal Society and the Royal Geographical Society.
The Royal Society insisted that the command of the
Antarctic Expedition should be entrusted to the
Director of the Civilian Staff of the expedition. The
Royal Geographical Society held that a naval officer
ought to command. Lieutenant R. F. Scott, R.N., is
the naval commander of the expedition.

THE RECENT EXTENSIVE
ROBBERIES.
RECOVERY OF THIS STOLEN PROPERTY
In connection with the recent robbery of copper,
tin, and other metal, valued at £55, from the premises of Davis, Shepherd, and Co., of Petersham,
and also of the finished and unfinished boots and
dressed leather which was stolen last Friday night
from Mr F.J. Walters' boot factory, Parramattaroad, Forrest Lodge, the police have been able to recover the whole of the stolen property, and also to
effect the arrest of several persons who are
alleged to be connected with the thefts.
It seems that on Tuesday last, acting on
certain information, Constable Hind, of the Redfern police, proceeded to a certain smelting works,
and after remaining there for some hours a man
made his appearance with a load of copper and tin,
which has since been identified as portion of
the property stolen from the premises of Davis,
Shepherd, and Co., at Petersham. Hind arrested
this man, and, after locking him up, proceeded to
his residence, where he secured a quantity of books.
From statements that were made to Hind, the latter
telephoned to the Redfern police station for assistance,
and Constables Moore, Whitehair, and Urquhart
arrived. Together the police went to a cottage in the
district of Waterloo, and there they found the whole
of the goods which had been stolen from the boot
factory at Forest Lodge, and also portion of the
goods stolen at Petersham. They then made several
other arrests. The persons charged, who included
a woman, were brought before the Redfern Police
Court yesterday, and were remanded for a week.
Last evening Detective Bannan made a further
arrest in connection with the matter.

A HALF-CASTE'S CONFESSION.

girl, who is about 23 years of age, made a statement at the inspector's office, the effect of which was

identity, carried on dugong fishing about Fraser
Island. The tragedy occurred at Poonah, near Boonooroo. A constable and the girl have gone to the
scene of the tragedy.

PHOENIX WHARF RESUMPTION.
---
THE ARBITRATOR'S AWARD.
Yesterday the Commissioners of the Land Appeal
Court, Messrs A. Oliver (president), C. Brandis, and
W. Houston, defended their decision in the case in
which they acted as arbitrators, viz., the Phoenix
Wharf resumption case.
The terms of agreement between the Sydney
Harbour Trust Commissioners and the Illawarra
Steam Navigation Company were detailed. From these it appeared that the wharf
property which was the property of the company
was resumed by proclamation on May 3, 1900, and
vested in the Minister for Works. The company
had since that date remained in occupation of portion
of the property. On December 1 1900, the Minister
for Works and the company mutually decided that
until an agreement as to the rent to be paid by the
company, or until the determination of their
occupancy they should pay to the Crown £1 per
month on account, and that in the event
of the parties not agreeing, the rent
was to be determined by the arbitrators
(the Land Appeal Court). The arbitrators
were therefore asked to determine the amount to be
paid by the company for rent or occupation from
the date of resumption until the determination of
the occupancy of the premises by the company. The
parties agreed to consider the Court's decision absolutely final and binding upon them, and to bear their
own costs in the matter of the agreement. The
Court said: ''We award, order, and determine
that the amount to be paid by the Illawarra
S. N. Company to the Crown for rent or
occupation of the land and premises or any
part thereof occupied by the company at Darling
Harbour shall be at the rate of £1900 sterling per
annum inclusive of rates and insurance, from the
date of the resumption to the determination of the
occupancy of the land and premises by the company,
which period we determine to be three years and
28 days."
Evidence in the arbitration case extended over
eight days, and a vast amount of evidence was tendered. The award was in favour of the company's
contentions.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.14784000:
REMEMBER THE CIVIL SERVANTS.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD.
Sir — Whenever there is a so-called surplus
in the accounts of the State Treasurer or
the Railway Commissioners, there is a host of
applicants for concessions which would soon
dissipate the whole of the money. In your
issue of Thursday a correspondent, "Henry
Brooke," asks that now the State is prosperous, the salaries of Public servants should
be restored to the figures ruling before the
days of retrenchment and economy. Apparently he does not realise that 15 years ago
this country was conducting its affairs, both
industrial and governmental, on an extravagant basis, which, as the crisis of 1893 proved,
could not continue without bankruptcy. Since
then all classes have had to accept less money
for services; interest in the bank has fallen
from 5 to 3 per cent. — a fall of 40 per cent, in
income; house rents have come down 25 per
cent, while salaries, commissions, and profits
of general business have been similarly reduced. So the Civil servant is not the only
person who has to put up with a smaller income, but he, like other consumers, finds his
money to-day will go further in hiring house
room, in cost of provisions, tramfares, etc.,
than it did in the extravagant times of two
decades ago.
Your correspondent, however, ignores the
fact that Mr. Carruthers intends to use the
surplus in the only way justified by the circumstances. The £900,000 in credit really
consists of the proceeds of land sales, which
is not true revenue, but is a portion of the
State capital too long employed to bolster up
a wasteful method of government. Henceforward this money is to be kept separate from
the revenue, and used like loan funds for
making reproductive works.
Civil Service rewards may be now lower
than those ruling here in years gone by but
they are very much higher than those given in
other countries abroad, or even in the neighbouring State of Victoria. I am etc.,
TAXPAYER.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15030000:
ESCAPEES FROM CASTLEMAINE.
A SURRENDER.
SECRETED IN A GOODS TRAIN.
MELBOURNE, Tuesday.
Harrison Goodhind, one of the three prisoners who escaped from Castlemaine Gaol on
Sunday night, surrendered himself to the Carlton police to-day. After making their escape
the men struck out into the bush, and tra-
velled hard all night. They had some bread
having saved their rations on Sunday. The
trio boarded a goods train at Taradale. Goodhind got in one part of the train, his companions in another. It was arranged that
the three escapees should got out at Sunshine, but this was not carried out. The train
stopped for half an hour at Woodend, and
it is supposed that Meakin and Brown left
there, and have made for the north-eastern
district. Goodhind came on to Melbourne in
the train without being discovered, and
dropped down from it unobserved a short distance from the city. He then went to his
home at North Fitzroy. Whilst on his way
to his home he was noticed by Constable Clinnick, who saw he answered to the description
of one of the wanted men, and followed him
to the house. The officer saw him enter the
back gate, and came up close behind him.
When Goodhind got inside the yard he locked
the back gate and rushed through the house.
When the officer got round to the front of the
house he saw Goodhind a couple of hundred
yards away, and started in pursuit. Goodhind
then visited Carlton police station and gave
himself up. He told his mother that he was
very sorry for what he had done, but he was
led away by others older than himself.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15194000:
MR. WADE'S RETURN.
HIS EXPERIENCE AS MOTORIST.
The Premier returned to town on Friday
with his faith in motor cars rudely shaken,
and with the sympathy that comes of understanding for the Government Whip, who on
one memorable occasion found it necessary to
leave a comfortable seat in the State car and
join in a ten-mile push to the nearest hotel.
Anxious to inspect the big Berembed weir,
the Premier, while on his way from Narrandera to Coolamon by motor caused a detour
to be made. Berembed was safely reached,
and the big works were inspected, but when
the car was headed southward and pace got
up, soft patches of red soil, in places under
water, gave trouble. In one of these patches
the car sank to the axles, and remained there
for an hour. Pine trees for a hundred yards
round were denuded of their lower branches,
and the soft road packed with bushes, in the
hope that the wheels as they were sent revolving round would get a grip. But to no
purpose. Chauffeur and passengers, politicians of high estate, and pressmen
toiled and sweated as they strained
with heavy poles to lever the car out of
the mud, and consigned to oblivion a group
of laughing jackasses which from the topmost
boughs of a neighbouring tree seemed to make
merry over man's misfortunes. Then a swaggie happened along, and stood, smoking his
pipe, in solemn silence, as he watched the
work going forward to get the car running.
Once out of the difficulty, speed regulations
were set at nought by the chief lawmaker, and
the car went flying on to Coolamon, some 20
miles distant. But before many miles had
been covered the car was again axle deep
this time in a broad ditch, which stretched
across the whole width of road. The Premier went hot afoot to a neighbouring farm
and enlisted the help of the farmer, who arrived on the scene with plough-horse and
chain gear. But no plough that horse had
ever drawn was so unyielding as the Premier's
car. Mr. Wade was already overdue at Coolamon, and he had visions of injury to the Liberal cause if he failed to keep his appointment
with the electors. He tramped along towards
the town of Mattong, where he was overtaken
by the car. Again the motor flew on its way
to Coolamon, but four miles out of the town
it went down into a deep ditch. The Premier
gave it up, borrowed a bicycle from a stranger,
and put in some fast pedalling. His troubles
ended just outside Coolamon, where he met
with a reception that helped towards philosophic acceptance of his past troubles.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.14678000:
PERSONAL.
M. Leon Caron, the well-known musical
conductor, died at the Gresham Hotel, near
the Town Hall, at 2 o'clock yesterday
morning. Towards the end of the Gilbert
Sullivan season, which terminated at her
Majesty's Theatre last February, M. Caron
suffered from a severe attack of dropsy, and
when he courageously insisted upon embarking with the company for New Zealand, few
people thought he would reach that country
alive. After two operations, however, he recovered sufficiently to resume work for a
time, but eventually it was deemed better
that he should return for rest in Sydney. He
arrived here about ten days ago, and although
a further operation was successfully performed by his medical adviser. Dr. M'Carthy,
he gradually sank. By his death Mr. J. C. Williamson loses his principal musical conductor,
and the genial French musician will
be widely mourned. He conducted the Royal
Comic Opera Company for many years, and
must have directed a repertoire of some two
score different works. M. Leon Caron was born
in 1S50 at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where he studied
music under Alexandre Guilmant, and the first
of the world's organists corresponded with him
affectionately throughout his life. M. Caron's
talent was so remarkable that he was sent
by the Boulogne Municipal Council to the
Paris Conservatoire, where he won distinction as a violinist and composer, but the close
of his studies was broken by the outbreak of
the war with Germany. This was an un-
fortunate crisis for the students, as the Prix
de Rome, for which young Caron stood in with
two others for the committee's final award,
was not bestowed that year (1870). M. Caron
fled to London during the Commune, and
was engaged as first violin of Riviere's orchestra at the Alhambra Theatre; and 12
months later he joined the famous orchestra
of Theodore Thomas in America, and remained with it until it was disbanded after
the Philadelphia Exhibition in 1876. At the
end of that year M. Caron made his debut
at the Melbourne Opera House, and then accepted the post of conductor of Lyster's
Grand Italian Opera Company, which he directed until 1880. A little later M. Caron
won the prize of 100 guineas offered by the
Commissioners of the Melbourne International
Exhibition for an original cantata, and his
"Victoria" was accordingly performed under
his direction by a chorus of 1000 voices and
an orchestra of 125 players at the ceremonious
opening of the Exhibition on October 1, 1880.
After the Exhibition M. Caron, as conductor
of English opera, produced for the first time
in Australia in English, "Carmen," "Mignon," "Paul et Virginie" (by Victor Masse),
"Fra Diavolo," "Rose of Castile," and many
other works. Since April, 1889, when he
directed the first performance of "The Yeomen of the Guard," M. Caron's energy and
talent maintained the high musical efficiency
for which the Royal Comic Opera Company
became celebrated under his baton. During
his long career in Australia, the late M. Leon
Caron married the Tasmanian soprano, Miss
Tasma Sherwin, nearly related to Mme. Amy
Sherwin. Mme. Caron, who nursed her husband devotedly to the last, and their young
daughter Irma, who made her stage debut
this year as the midshipmite in "H.M.S.
Pinafore," survive the esteemed musician.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15344000:
PUBLIC LIBRARIAN.
-»-
OFFER TO MR. IFOULD.
MR. CARMICHAEL'S ATTITUDE.
The trustees of the Free Public Library,
preparatory to making a recommendation to
the Minister for Education, have offered the
vacant position of librarian to Mr. W. H.
Ifould, chief librarian of Adelaide, at a salary
of £630 per annum, but he has not yet decided whether he will accept or reject the
offer.
Mr. Carmichael, Minister for Education,
stated last night that no recommendation had
yet reached him from the trustees.
Correspondence took place a month ago between the Minister for Education and the
trustees of the Free Public Library about the
appointment of a successor to Mr. F. W.
Bladen, who retired from the position of
librarian as far back as February. The
State Government passed by the nominee of
the trustees, and asked for some other nomination. For some time Dr. Watson, who is
a trustee of the Institution, has been acting
as librarian, and it was generally understood
that his co-trustees were desirous that he
should be permanently appointed to the post.
Mr. Carmichael took the point that with the
trustees lay the nomination, but that the appointment had to be made by the Governor
in-Council. Any nomination, therefore, had
to receive his official approval. He said that
he did not regard Dr. Watson as the best
nomination available, and he asked the trustees to send in another name.
Professor MacCallum, who is chairman of the
library trustees, regarded the action of Mr.
Carmichael, in allowing the facts of the case
at that stage to get into the press, as a grave
breach of etiquette. He thought that they
at least should have had the Minister's decision placed before them first of all.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15590000:
RECKLESS DASH.
AUSTRALASIANS DISDAIN
COVER.
CHARGING AHEAD.
ATHENS, May 10.
An eye witness of the recent fighting
states that the heaviest losses were borne
by the Australians and New Zealanders,
whose one fault was a complete disdain for
cover. Their bravery and dash were amazing.
In some cases men, after rushing the first
Turkish trenches for 10 minutes charged
ahead, despite the appeals of their officers,
penetrating several miles inland, and suffering heavily, when Turkish reinforcements compelled them to retreat.
Home troops pay the warmest tributes to
the Australians.
German officers endeavoured to create a
diversion by donning uniforms of English
and Australasian officers, mingling with our
men, and giving false orders.

PATRIOTIC NATIVES.
-
Mr. K. C. Eliot, Resident Commissioner in
the Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony, who is
in Sydney on official business, states that
when the native constabulary of the Islands,
comprising about sixty men, heard of the
serious war news about six weeks ago, a
considerable number of them waited upon
him, and requested that they should be allowed to go to the war. He obtained the
necessary permission, and shortly a body of
thirty, representing half the force, would
arrive in New Zealand under Mr. Burge, who
had volunteered to accompany them to the
front, and they would proceed to the war with
the native troops from the Dominion. Since
the war commenced the residents of the
group have contributed £12,000 to patriotic
funds, and, the white community being very
small, it was a safe estimate, to say that
£10,000 of this amount had been contributed
by the natives, the total population being
about 35.000.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15808000:
DEATH OF MS. A. W. HAMBLY.
The death of Mr. Anthony Warren Hambly
took place at his residence, in Elswick-street,
Leichhardt, at the age of 80 years. In his
earlier years the late Mr. Hambly followed
mining and grazing pursuits in the Grenfell
district. He came to Australia from England
when about 20 years old. While gold-mining
at Grenfell he made a very successful find
at a place called O'Brien's Reef. He subsequently went in for grazing, and owned the
station known in the Grenfell locality as
Ipswich. After having spent about a quarter
of a century at Grenfell, where he took a live
interest in all public matters, he came to
Sydney, where he has led a retired life. He
is survived by a widow, three sons, and five
daughters. One son was killed in the Boer
war. The funeral takes place this afternoon,
leaving his late residence for the Anglican
portion of the Rookwood Cemetery, where the
interment will be made.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.15795000:
DEATH OF MR. J. HERRMANN.
The death occurred on Saturday last at his
home Rossmore, Wardell-road, Dulwich Hill,
of Mr. Jacob Herrmann, late outdoor superintendent of the New South Wales Tramways.
The deceased was for many years in the
tramway service, from which illness necessitated his retirement recently. He was 56
years of age. The funeral took place on Monday, and was
very largely attended. From deceased's late
residence to Lewisham railway station the
cortege was headed by the Tramway Band
and about 200 tramway officers and employees.
At the cemetery a short service was held in
the Roman Catholic Church, conducted by
the Rev. Father E. J. M'Namara, who also
officiated at the grave.
The chief mourners were Mrs. Herrmann,
(widow), Messrs. H. and L. Herrmann (sons),

Digby (brother-in-law and sister), Messrs. L.
and H. Herrmann (nephews), Mrs. Haddock,
and Miss H. Herrmann (nieces), Mrs. E. Herrmann (sister-in-law), and Mr. and Mrs. H.
Ross.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16163000:
CITRUS SHIPMENTS.
The steamer Jervis Bay, which leaves
Sydney to-day, is carrying the last consignment of fresh fruit for the British Empire
Exhibition. This consignment consists of
76 cases donated by the Central Mangrove
Citrus Packing House Ltd., and the Maroota,
Glenorie, and Kenthurst branches of the
Fruitgrowers' Association of New South
Wales.
Although this shipment is a few cases
short of the total requirements, it is the
only one which has been so. Considering
that this State has supplied nearly twice its
original quota, owing to supplies from
Queensland not having been forthcoming, the
growers who have interested themselves in
the matter must be congratulated.
The same steamer is also carrying 350
cases of citrus fruit from the New South
Wales Central Citrus Association, Ltd., made
up of consignments of Navels, Silettas, and
Parramatta, from the Wyong, Gosford, Central Mangrove, and Somersby citrus packing
houses, and from Mr. F. A. Nicolson, of
Glenorie.
The results of this shipment will be eagerly
looked for, particularly as to the keeping
qualities of Silettas and Parramattas, and
their suitability for the English.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16174000:
DRIVER'S MISTAKE.
HOLIDAY PARTY ENDANGERED.
A serious accident was averted on Saturday night, when, on the Camden-road, about
two miles from Cambelltown, a motor lorry,
driven by F. Hopkins, of Leichhardt, and containing a large party of excursionists, was
travelling along the road, when a portion of
road under reconstruction necessitated a
deviation. The driver inadvertently ran
across an open paddock. Suddenly the lorry
raced down a sharp decline into a deep gully,
and Hopkins, realising that he had made a
mistake, forced the brakes on. The lorry
struck the bottom and tilted over on one
side, hurtling its crowd of holiday-makers into
a heap. Luckily the vehicle did not turn
completely over.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16119000:
CASUALTIES.
------------
DROWNING CASES.
Believed to have taken a fit and fallen into
the water, Thomas Sterling, 23 years of age, of
Hillcote-crescent, Manly, was found drowned
near the rocks at Fairlight yesterday. He
left his home on the previous evening to go
fishing at Fairlight, and owing to his not returning that night a search was made yesterday. Sergeant Dale, of the Manly police,
found portion of the young man's clothing on
the rocks and a piece of fishing line, and
hidden in seaweed nearby he found the body.
It is stated that Sterling was subject to fits,
and the police believe that he was overcome
by an attack whilst fishing near the water's
edge.
ALBURY, Sunday.
Thomas Benjamin O'Donnell a labourer,
aged 60, who was making down the river to
Moama to secure employment on the railway
construction works, was drowned in the
Murray yesterday afternoon, near the Gooranadda Hotel, on the Victorian side, opposite
Howlong.
He was on the bank of the river, when he
is supposed to have taken a fit. He was
seen to fall backwards into shallow water,
but was not seen again. Dragging operations
were undertaken by Constable Bartholomew,
of Howlong, and Constables Bell and Barnett,
of Albury, but the body had not been recovered at 9 p.m.
One brother of O'Donnell, John O'Donnell,
resides in Wodonga, and another in Albury.
KYOGLE. Monday.
Yesterday at Wyangarie a man named Craigie met his death by drowning in the river.
He had been working for a local farmer for
some time, and was 65 years of age.

LONDON, Oct. 11.
The first public lecture given by Mr. Horatio
Bottomley since his release from prison attracted thousands to Queen's Hall. Prolonged
cheers greeted his reading of a letter from
the foreman of the Jury at his trial, saying,
"It was a cruel sentence, and it came as a
great surprise to me and other members of the
jury. We had not expected anything like it.
Our opinion was that you had no intention
of defrauding anyone."

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16285000:
SCHOOL-CHURCH AT SANS SOUCI
The foundation-stone of a new Roman
Catholic school-church, to be built with a
frontage to Broughton-Street, Sans Souci, was
recently placed in position. The walls of the
building are of brickwork, the exterior walling being cavity, and of sufficient thickness
to enable an extra story being added at a
later date. The foundations are of reinforced
concrete. The total length of the building
will be 60 feet by a width of 30 feet. This
space can be divided into three class-rooms
by the means of folding partitions. In addition to this floor area there is a brick sanctuary, provided at one end, with a sacristy
for the clergy. Along one side of the building, which will be roofed with tiles, a 10 feet
wide verandah is provided. The elevations
are of a neat design, and the construction
is in O.K. bricks, with cement dressings. The
work is being carried out by Messrs. S. Patrick
and Sons, builders, of Bexley, to designs
prepared by Mr. Austin McKay, architect.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16415000:
WOMBEYAN CAVES.
MITTAGONG, Thursday.
The new road to the Wombeyan Caves is
almost completed. At the caves considerable
improvements have been executed, including
the installation of electric light. The proposed road from the Jenolan to the Wombeyan
Caves has been surveyed and levels are being
taken. This road, instead of following the old
track over the Abercrombie Range, thus including many steep grades, keeps to the ridge
of the mountains, which offers a splendid
gravel surface and few hills. Increasing numbers of tourists are utilising Mittagong as
a starting point for the caves, which are 43
miles away.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16079000:
PERSONAL.
VICE-REGAL.
His Excellency the Governor-General, attended by Captain the Hon. C. Mulholland,
C.B.E., D.S.O., military secretary, and Lieuten-
ant W. J. Seymour, A.D.C., R.N., will arrive in
Sydney this morning by the Melbourne express.
Her Excellency Lady Forster, attended by
Captain Alan Lawrence, A.D.C., was present at
the Junior Red Cross pageant at the Town Hall
yesterday evening.
Dame Margaret Davidson, attended by Miss
Henderson, opened the Junior Red Cross exhibition at the Town Hall yesterday afternoon.
Mr. and Mrs. Lionel Manchee and Miss Manchee were the guests of his Excellency and
Dame Margaret Davidson to luncheon yesterday.
Dr. Earle Page, the Federal Treasurer, who
arrived from Melbourne yesterday, was suffering from a severe cold, and went direct to
Strathfield, where he was confined to his home
all day.
Senator Gardiner (N.S.W.) was reappointed
leader, Senator M'Dougall (N.S.W.) deputy
leader, and Senator Needham (W.A.) party
whip, at a meeting of the Labour senators in
Melbourne yesterday.
The Chief Justice (Sir Wm. Cullen) and Lady
Cullen will leave Sydney to-night for Mudgee,
where the winter holiday will be spent.
Mr. Peter Board, late Director of Education,
is at present on a visit to Adelaide, where he
is inquiring into matters relating to technical
and apprenticeship education.
Mr. W. H. Atherton, managing director of
Turner, Atherton, and Co., Ltd., hatters' engineers, of Stockport, England, and also a
director of the Stockport Ring Spinning Co.,
Ltd., is at present on a short visit to Australia
for health reasons. He Is staying in Sydney,
but will leave for England again on July 21
by the Ascanius.
Mr. Paul Marcus, who has been Vice-Consul
for France in Sydney for many years, and who
has been transferred to Shanghai, will make
his departure in a few days.
The Boyd Dunlop Morehead Exhibition for

the Sydney Grammar School to Sydney University this year, tenable for three years, has
been awarded to Victor Radcliff Webb, only
son of Mr. J. M. Webb, of Parliament House.
Mr. Reg. Powell, Australasian advertising
manager for Perdriau Rubber Co., Ltd., who

was the recipient of a case of cutlery and
silver, and a complete smoker's outfit, from his
fellow employees.
Mr. A. O. Manning, M.P., has been elected
representative of New South Wales at the interstate Pastoral Conference, to be held in
Melbourne next week, regarding the British
Empire Exhibition.
Mr. M. E. Tilnay, who was formerly a Commissioner of Repatriation in New South Wales,
has assumed the duties of his new office as a
member of the Victorian Repatriation Commission.
Mr. C. H. P. Robinson has been appointed
principal Parliamentary reporter on the Federal "Hansard" staff, to succeed Mr. B. H.
Friend, who has retired from the position. Mr.
W. Adams has been appointed second Parliamentary reporter.
Mr. Geo. H, James, district superintendent
for Messrs. Allen Taylor and Co., accompanied by Mrs. James, left Sydney on Thursday
by the Niagara on a tour of inspection of
British Columbia and the Pacific Coast of
America.
Senator E. J. Russell (Vic), who has been
in ill-health for some weeks, has been granted
two months' leave of absence by the Senate.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16484000:

Judge White presided at the Singleton
Quarter Sessions, which concluded yesterday.
Michael Joseph Maher was charged with
breaking and entering the premises of Henry
William Bourke, mercer, and stealing a quantity of goods valued at £48, and with having

William Ernest McTaggart, a grazier, of

guilty.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16477000:
AMUNDSEN.
STILL MISSING.
LONDON, July.
The correspondent of the British United
Press at Tromsoe telegraphed to London to-
day; "It is reported that Captain Amundsen
has been rescued near the south coast of
Spitzbergen by the British yacht Albion."
Since receipt of the foregoing message,
however, the Albion, which is north of Tromsoe, reports having picked up by wireless the
information broadcast from England that it
had discovered the missing explorer.
A report from Oslo says that the committee
organising the search for Amundsen declined
the offer of British light planes, owing to
the delay that would take place in them
reaching Tromsoe.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16593000:
CALL THE AMBULANCE.
DANGER OF UNSKILLED
TREATMENT.
When people are injured it is not advisable to transport them to hospital in private
vehicles if ambulance facilities are available.
The secretary of the New South Wales
Ambulance Transport Board (Mr. J. L. R.
Cameron) said yesterday that in the case of
accident the proper procedure was to telephone for the ambulance. Ambulance stations were open day and night ready to render
assistance to the injured or sick. Owing to
unskilled treatment a simple fracture might
become a compound fracture, thus endangering a limb, or frequently the life of the

MEMORIAL TO JOHN BAXTER.
PERTH. Thursday.
The Western Australian Historical Society
has decided to erect a tablet on a cairn between Eucla and Esperance to the memory
of John Baxter, the explorer, a companion
of Edward John Eyre, who was killed on the
spot by a native on April 29, 1841. Mr.
John W. W. Graham, who has undertaken
to affix the tablet, was the boy of the party
which, in 1882, found Baxter's remains.
Eyre and Baxter, with two New South
Wales natives and one from Western Australia, left Port Eyre, South Australia, for
Albany, and, when camped about 40 miles
west of Eyre, Western Australia. Baxter was
shot by one of the New South Wales blacks.
During Eyre's absence, two blacks decamped
with two guns and most of the rations.
Baxter died soon after the return of Eyre,
who left the body covered with a blanket on
the stony ground, and, after great privations,
with the Western Australian black reached
the coast near Esperance, where he was picked
up by a French whaling boat.
The site of the tragedy is about 15 miles
south of the trans-Australian car route.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16721000:
CAPTAIN COOK'S VOYAGES.
"Captain Cook and his Naturalists" was
the subject of a lantern lecture given before
the Naturalists' Society of New South Wales
by Mr. Tom Iredale, conchologist to the Australian Museum. Mr. Iredale declared that
Sir Joseph Banks, rather than Captain Cook,
was the father of Australia. Cook was purely
a navigator, whereas Banks, as a naturalist
and an artist, was deeply impressed with natural phenomena, and in turn impressed others
with the subjects which he had studied.
Cook had taken down word for word in his
log book what Banks and Solander had told
him. Hence the common mistake often made
that Cook himself was a naturalist.

IN PROBATE.
(Before Mr. Justice Harvey.)
WILL OF AMY JONES.
By order of February 3 Alice Mary Wentworth, caveatrix, was directed to show cause
why probate should not be granted to the
Perpetual Trustee Company of the will of
Amy Jones, made on September 6, 1928, and
it was further ordered that a document dated
January 5, 1931, purporting to be the last
will of deceased, should be propounded by
the persons named in the order.
By her will of 1928 testatrix made alternative devices and bequests in favour of her
adopted son to meet the position created by
any possible judgment of the Court of Appeal
regarding the estate of her deceased husband.
The document of January, 1931, was found
near her body when on January 6 she was
discovered dead in her residence at Kogarah.
Her death was a mystery, but was generally
attributed to heart failure, injuries to the head
having been caused by falling on to the stove
in the kitchen. By the will executed on
the previous day, Mrs. Jones left all her real
and personal estate to her brothers and sisters,
except a bequest of £500 to Mrs. Wentworth,
and two small bequests to others. The document purported to have been witnessed by "J.
T. Scott" and "A. Carmichael." All efforts
to discover these persons had since proved
fruitless.
On the matter now being called it was stated
that the relatives of testatrix did not propose
to enter upon a suit, but would submit all
the facts to the Court. The caveatrix did
not contest probate, but would make submissions as to costs.
The reading of documents had not concluded when the Court adjourned.
Mr. J. R. Nield (instructed by Messrs. Sly
and Russell) appeared for the trustees; Mr. T.
T. Henery (instructed by Messrs. Rowley,
Roseby, and Co.) for certain relatives; and Mr.
E. R. Mann for the caveatrix.

BIGAMY CHARGE.
Amazing Defence.
JUDGE DISCHARGES JURY.
MELBOURNE, Thursday.
Mr. Justice Wasley told a jury to-day that
there had not been such startling developments in the Criminal Court for many years
as those which occurred at the trial of William Leslie Edmund Penney, 31, salesman,
on a charge of bigamy.
Penney was charged under the name of
Billy Edwards, and the Crown Prosecutor
(Mr. Book) alleged that he had gone through
the ceremony of marriage with a young woman
at Trafalgar in August, 1930, while his wife
by a previous marriage, which was said to
have taken place at Drouin in April, 1930,
was living.
The trial ended by Mr. Justice Wasley discharging the jury, and remanding Edwards
to allow the Crown to investigate his defence.
The defence had evoked sharp comments
from Mr. Justice Wasley yesterday. Mr.
Stretton, who defended Edwards, had declared that the charge must fail, because
neither of the marriages referred to by the
Crown was lawful, as Edwards had had a
prior marriage in 1921.
Mr. Justice Wasley would not allow a certificate of that marriage to be admitted as
evidence, neither would he allow Edwards's
mother to be recalled to testify that the
woman whom Edwards was said to have
married in 1921 was still alive.
When the trial was resumed to-day, however, Mr. Justice Wasley said that he thought
that he should allow Edwards's mother to be
recalled. Mr. Stretton had made a slip
inadvertently, and he should be allowed to
correct it.
Mr. Stretton: I have better evidence now.
The real wife is here.
This woman, called as a witness, said that
she had married Edwards in September, 1921,
and they had separated after 15 months.
Mr. Justice Wasley discharged the jury,
and remanded Edwards.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.16619000:
AMAZING VOYAGE.
Schooner Adrift in
Hurricane.
SWEPT ACROSS ATLANTIC.
WOMAN PASSENGER'S ORDEAL.
(British Official Wireless.)
LONDON, Jan. 18.
The three-masted British schooner
Neptune, of St. John's, Newfoundland,
a wooden vessel of 126 tons, has been
towed into Tobermory Bay, on the west
coast of Scotland by the lighthouse
steamer Hesperus, after remarkable adventures.
She was literally blown across the
Atlantic in the wrong direction.
The Neptune left St John's on November
29 on a coastal voyage of 100 miles to Newtown, Bonavista Bay, Newfoundland. She
was within 30 miles of her intended port
when she was compelled by head winds to
make for the open sea. Her complement consisted of the captain, mate, a crew of three,
and five passengers, including one woman.
Without warning came a hurricane, before
which the ship was driven helplessly. The
captain had no idea of his bearings. With
boats and bulwarks smashed, the deckhouse
washed away, and only two spokes left in the
steering wheel, the Neptune was at the mercy
of the mountainous seas for seven weeks.
The vessel was well provisioned, but there
was anxiety that the water might run out,
which eventually became a grave possibility.
At last a rocky coast was seen ahead. It was
Ardnamurchan Point. The schooner's distress was observed from the lighthouse, which
signalled to the steamer Hesperus.
CAPTAIN'S STORY.
(Copyright .— Australian Press Association)
"After the storm I had no idea of my position," said Captain Job K. Barkow. "My
knowledge of navigation is limited to my usual
route and I am seldom out of sight of land.
Therefore, although a large steamer gave us
a course, I was little the wiser. We picked
up a light, which I thought was Eddystone, on
January 14, but it was Skerrymore, on the
west coast of Scotland. We lived on the
cargo of fruit, but the water was rationed to
a glass per day."
Mrs Humphreys, the wife of one of the
crew, said that for long periods she was confined to the forecastle with the men. It was
impossible to remain aft, owing to tremendous seas.
Four out of the ten men on board were
passengers bound for Newtown, Newfoundland.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.17242000:
ETHEL TURNER'S ACHIEVEMENTS.
Recognition by Fellow Writers.
Ethel Turner, the famous Australian author of "Seven Little Australians,"
and more than a score of other children's books, holds the key to a children's paradise in which grown-ups are allowed to roam. To recognise her
literary achievement the Fellowship of Australian Writers will entertain her
at luncheon at Farmer's Blaxland Galleries on June 25.
Mrs.
H. R. CURLEWIS (ETHEL TURNER) looks at the world from the
window of her Mosman home.
IN private life, the story-teller is Mrs. H
R Curlewis, wife of Judge Curlewis. To
meet her you see a blue-eyed bustling little
person with greying hair and a pink and
white complexion many a girl would envy.
She keeps that fresh outlook on life which
has made so much of the charm of her writing during the past 40 years. Mrs Curlewis
is a gracious woman with a fine sense of
humour and a real understanding of boys and
girls.
Her home is on the shores of Sydney Harbour looking towards the sea. This children's
story-teller was born near Doncaster in Yorkshire, but since her arrival from England
when she was eight years of age her life has
become merged in the stream of Australian
life and literature.
She was educated at that famous square
brick building in Elizabeth-street Sydney, the
Girls' High School-which has nourished so
many bright hopes and efforts. Even at
school Ethel Turner wrote stories; with her
sister, Lilian, she edited "Iris," a schoolgirls'
magazine.
Busy Literary Pen.
MRS. CURLEWIS'S real literary life com-
menced when she wrote her "Children's
Page" in the "Illustrated Sydney News." In
1894 "Seven Little Australians" was published,
and since then the busy pen has never rested.
This year she contributed one of the reddest
chapters to "Murder Pie," a collaborated effort
by several Australian writers.
More than a million copies of "Seven Little
Australians" have been sold. That it is a story
for all ages and all peoples is indicated by
the fact that it has been translated into
Danish, Norwegian, Swedish, Dutch, French,
and Czechoslovakian.
An Example for Authors.
THE quiet persistence of this small figure at
her desk writing destroying, destroying
and working again perfecting style and plot
and winning at last a well-deserved success
holds a lesson for many an ambitious author.
Mrs. Curlewis found it no trouble to write a
book a year and with one or two exceptions
all her books have been about children.
"Some days indeed," she has confessed, "the
pen will not write. You sit down and make
sketches on the blotting paper. But as a rule
I went to my room about ten o clock and
by noon or so I had done my days work. So
many days work to a chapter, so many chapters to a book—a regular literary arithmetic."
Interrupted Arithmetic
SOMETIMES the arithmetic in the early
days was not so easy for a son and daughter intercepted the methodical dip into the ink-
bottle. Now there are a grandson and grand-
daughter to read her books and demand more
of the favourite characters.
In the midst of writing her thirty-odd books
Mrs. Curlewis —who was one of the first
people to write books for children without a
moral —has found time to surf, play tennis
and golf, and potter about the lovely garden
of her home. At the moment the garden wins
over the ink-pot but one suspects that Mrs.
Curlewis is still very much in love with ''Seven
Little Australians;" perhaps the three-year-
old Phillipa and the five year-old Ian will
soon persuade their grandmother to write
more about the lovable Judy.

Knight and Clarence Patrick Booth, he
assaulted Norman Collyer and robbed him

table, and he himself had borne a good

William Sydney Francis Knight, 31, cleaner,
and William Raines, 31, clerk, pleaded not
guilty to a charge of assaulting Rudolph
Weber, at Manly, on July 18, with intent to
rob him.
Weber, a pastrycook, stated that two men
suddenly attacked him in a lane off the Corso,

CAR FATALITY.
Finding of Accidental Death.
POLICEMAN EXONERATED.
A finding of accidental death was returned
by the City Coroner, Mr. Oram, at the conclusion yesterday of an inquest on Albert
Victor Anderson, 45, electric meter fixer, of
Rose Street, North Bondi, who died in hospital on May 28, shortly after having been
struck by a car in Old South Head Road,
near Warner's Avenue, Rose Bay.
The car was driven by Constable William
Aloysius O'Rourke, of No. 2 Police Station,
Sydney, who was accompanied by Constable
Arthur William Manley, of the same station.
The coroner said that he was satisfied that
the tragedy was entirely an accident, and he
could not see that any blame was attachable
to the driver of the car.
The evidence showed that the locality was
badly lighted.
"This inquest has taken a long while,"
he added, "because there were many witnesses,
owing to the fact that the Police Department
is jealous of the reputation of its officers
and wants thorough investigations into matters concerning them."

LOAN TOUR
Repair Completed
The Lancaster bomber, which
came to Australia last July and
was badly damaged when landing at a northern New South
Wales town last October during
a Liberty Loan tour, passed
through Sydney on Saturday
from Melbourne on its way to
Brisbane.
The mishap in October was caused
by the machine's over-running a short
runway. It was stated at the time
that repairs would take too long to enable it to continue the loan tour to
Queensland.
The Minister for Air, Mr. Drakeford,
announced recently that repairs had
been nearly completed, and that the
Lancaster would begin a Victory Loan
tour in Queensland on April 17.

machine on the tour.
overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.17704000:
NOOGOORA BURR
Macquarie Marshes
Infested.
WARREN, Monday.
In view of the appalling infestation of the Macquarie Marshes by
noogoora burr, an appeal has been
made to Marthaguy Shire Council
to make representations to have
the marshes declared a quarantine
area.
Nearby settlers are faced with a very
difficult problem, the seed of the burr
being carried on to their properties from
the marshes by the periodical inundations of slow-spreading waters and the
thousands of travelling stock which leave
the marsh area annually heavily covered
with matured noogoora burr.
Writing to the shire council one of the
settlers Mr Roland Storm, of Killarney
pointed out that hired labour was out
of the question to deal with the burrs.
Very often the properties carried a certain amount of water, and at such times
wasps and hornets were to be found in
countless millions among the heavy
growths of lignum while wild pigs and
snakes were there in considerable numbers.
He quoted an instance when hired
labour beat a frantic retreat from a
continuous and concerted attack of mos-
quitoes. Mr. Storm stated that an in-
spection of the various routes travelled
by stock from the marsh area revealed
a plain trail of flourishing noogoora burr
plants.
The council decided to refer the matter
to the Department of Agriculture.

COLLISION
Narrabri Farmers
Injured

men were injured when a lorry
struck a train at a level crossing
on the Gunnedah road to-night.

overproof/en/hipe-ocrepair-bench_v1.0_ov.17855000:
ADVANCES ANNOUNCED
IN COMMUNIQUE
The communique from General MacArthur's headquarters
yesterday, announcing the new
advances, stated: -
In combined and co-ordinated operations, the forces of the South-west
Pacific and South Pacific areas have
advanced and expanded their bases of
deployment by occupying Nassau Bay,
on the north coast of New Guinea, the
Trobriand and Woodlark island groups,
and are attacking in the New Georgia
Group.
The occupation of the Trobriands
and the Woodlark area was successfully accomplished without opposition,
and apparently unbeknown to the
enemy.
In the New Georgia Group, our
forces have successfully landed on New
Georgia and Rendova Islands, and
are engaging the enemy's defences.
All elements, ground, naval, and air,
are being employed in closest synchronisation.
The forces of the two areas are
operating under their own commanders, the entire movement being
under the direction of the Commander-in-Chief, South-west Pacific Area.
NORTH-WESTERN SECTOR:
DARWIN. - Twenty-seven enemy
bombers, escorted by 21 fighters, raided
the area at midday, with some damage to ground installations and slight
casualties. Our fighters intercepted
and shot down six enemy bombers and
two fighters. Seven bombers and a
fighter were damaged. We lost six
planes in air combat.
TIMOR. - Lautem: Our medium
units bombed the aerodrome after
dark, starting fires.
Fuiloro: Our medium units, in a
night attack, bombed the aerodrome,
causing fires.
Koepang: Our medium bombers attacked Penfoei aerodrome after dark,
starting numerous large fires in dispersal areas.
NORTH-EASTERN SECTOR: -
NEW BRITAIN. - Rabaul: Our
heavy bombers attacked Vunukanau
and Lakunai aerodromes during the
night, dropping nearly 23 tons of high
explosives, fragmentation, and incen-
diary bombs throughout the dispersal
areas. Several explosions and numerous fires were observed, one visible for
100 miles. Heavy anti-aircraft fire
and some enemy night fighters were
encountered. One of our bombers is
missing.
Cape Gloucester: One of our heavy
units, on armed reconnaissance, under
difficult weather conditions, bombed
from mast-head height, and strafed
one of three 1,000-ton enemy cargo
ships in Dampier Strait, leaving it
sinking. Another of the vessels, after
being heavily machine-gunned, ap-
peared damaged, and deserted when
our aircraft departed.
NEW GUINEA. - Salamaua: Our
medium bombers, in support of
ground forces, heavily attacked enemy
positions, and supply installations near
the aerodrome and at Bobdubi.
